title: Resurrection
summary: The New Testament proclaims that God raised Jesus bodily on the third day. The Gospel accounts describe the empty tomb and encounters with the risen Jesus; Acts presents the claim in public preaching, and Paul argues that Jesus’ resurrection is the beginning and guarantee of the dead being raised. It is central to Christian proclamation because it presents Jesus as vindicated by God and grounds hope for life beyond death.
historical_context: Acts 2 presents Peter proclaiming Jesus’ resurrection in Jerusalem and reading Psalm 16 as hope that God would not abandon his faithful one to death. In 1 Corinthians 15, Paul says he is passing on a tradition that Jesus died, was buried, was raised, and appeared to witnesses. These passages show resurrection at the center of early Christian proclamation; they also show how the first Christians argued from Scripture and testimony.
ancient_near_east_context: The event is announced within a world where death was final, making the claim of bodily resurrection a startling theological and historical assertion.
literary_context: Matthew, Luke, and John each tell of the empty tomb and encounters with the risen Jesus, but shape the scenes differently: Matthew moves from the women at the tomb to Jesus’ meeting with the disciples in Galilee; Luke includes the road to Emmaus and the disciples’ recognition of Jesus; John follows Mary Magdalene’s encounter and Thomas’s response. Acts turns the resurrection into public proclamation, while Paul’s letters explain its implications for believers and the future raising of the dead.
covenantal_significance: The New Testament presents the resurrection as God’s vindication of Jesus and the beginning of a wider hope. Paul calls the risen Christ the “firstfruits” of those who have died (1 Corinthians 15:20–23), linking Jesus’ life to the future resurrection of others. Romans 6 uses this hope to explain why sharing in Christ’s death also means living a new life, while 1 Peter calls resurrection the basis of a living hope.
canonical_role: The resurrection joins Israel’s Scriptures to the New Testament’s claims about Jesus and future life. In Acts 2, Peter reads Psalm 16 in light of Jesus’ resurrection; in 1 Corinthians 15, Paul presents Jesus as the firstfruits of the coming resurrection. The Gospels narrate the empty tomb and appearances, Acts proclaims them, and the letters trace their consequences for Christian life and hope.

scripture_references.notes: union with Christ in death and life

interpretive_notes.note: Keep the bodily, historical claim in view; the New Testament does not treat resurrection as a metaphor only.
The resurrection is both the vindication of Jesus and the pattern for future resurrection.

common_questions: Why is the resurrection central to Christian faith?
How does resurrection relate to new creation?
